m24.title: Controls, harness and numerical mutation — frozen contract and independent oracle
m24.mentor: Before I trust an experiment, I test the experiment: a control that must pass, controls that must fail and tests of the harness itself. What does the runner do if the oracle throws an exception or returns NaN? This isn't theory: the runner in a real study ended up reporting oracle_valid: true with the oracle failed.
m24.kid: Before using a scale, you weigh something you already know the weight of. If the scale says something else, the problem is the scale.
obj: Include positive and negative controls in an experiment.
Test the harness: invalid baseline, NaN and oracle exceptions.
Mutate a numerical model with a frozen tolerance and an independent oracle.
m24.pre: The mutation testing and preregistration modules; Python.
theory: Positive control: what must pass (the exact solver, the clean case). Negative controls: one sabotaged variant of each kind, which must fail.
Test the harness: “an invalid baseline blocks its mutants”, “NaN is never PASS” and “an oracle exception is not a killed mutant”.
A real finding: in scientific-qa-evidence the runner reported oracle_valid: true when the oracle had failed (FINDINGS, finding 8).
Frozen contract: the tolerance (10⁻⁶) is set before running, and the oracle doesn't share a solver with the implementation.

The campaign: 84 paired variants across 9 physical models, with 27 PASS, 54 KILLED and 3 SURVIVED, the same on macOS and on Linux. The tiny mutation in the RC circuit survives and is left visible on purpose.
Separate cases from behaviors: the 54 KILLED correspond to 51 distinct behaviors.
hands: In scientific-qa-evidence/evidence/numerical/source, run python3 -m unittest -v test_runner.
Inject an oracle that returns float("nan") and check that it never yields PASS or KILLED.
Add a simple tenth model (free fall with linear drag) with its analytical oracle, two known mutants and one close to the threshold.
crit: Your harness has all three tests (invalid baseline, NaN, oracle exception) and all three pass.
The injected NaN never comes out PASS or KILLED.
The table separates cases from distinct behaviors.
If the mutant close to the threshold survives, it's reported as SURVIVED without lowering the tolerance.
m24.deliver: A harness with 3 tests of itself + a tenth model with an oracle and mutants + a verdict table.
m24.mut: Inject an oracle that returns NaN and check that it never yields PASS or KILLED.
m24.top: Your table separates cases from distinct behaviors and explains which mutants are equivalent.

m25.title: Fluid physics and statistics for the debugger
m25.mentor: You don't need to be a physicist to test a fluid model, but you do need to understand which law each check is watching. And you don't need to be a statistician to say whether a check ranks the error well, but you do need to know when a difference is noise.
m25.kid: Water won't let itself be squeezed and energy doesn't appear out of nowhere. The checker looks at whether the neural network follows those rules, like a referee who knows the rulebook.
obj: Explain which physical law each check (D1, D2, D3) watches and why D4 isn't a check.
Predict which check flags each sabotaged variant before running.
Use Spearman, cluster bootstrap and Wilson to decide whether a difference is noise.
m25.pre: The controls and harness module; basic vector calculus and numpy.
theory: Three laws watched by predictor-debugger's debugger: incompressibility (div u = 0, check D1), energy balance (kinetic energy only decays through viscosity, at a rate of ν·enstrophy, D2) and the momentum equation (Navier–Stokes residual, D3).
D4 is the error against the reference: it's used to judge the debugger, it's not one of the debugger's checks.
The design's controls: P0 is the exact solver (positive), P0f32 the same thing rounded to float32, P1 persistence, P2 the FNO, P3a breaks incompressibility and P3b injects energy.
What's being tested is the debugger, not the network: a poor network is an acceptable result; a debugger that can't tell the controls apart is a failure.
One-step versus rollout: in a rollout the network feeds on its own answers for 20 steps in a row and the errors pile up.
Spearman measures whether a check ranks the error well (ranks, not values). Cluster bootstrap: you resample trajectories, not steps; resampling steps gives narrower, misleading intervals.
Wilson interval: 27 out of 29 cases isn't just “93 %”, it's 93.1 % with an interval of 78–98 %.

res.label: Li et al. — Fourier Neural Operator

hands: Read predictor-debugger's DESIGN.md (System and Debugger checks) and pd/checks.py. Explain in your own words why D1 catches P3a and D2 catches P3b.

With the kit in round5/KIT.md (step 1), generate an exact pair and three sabotaged ones (energy ×1.05, added gradient, shifted phase) and predict which check should flag each one BEFORE running. Use saved mode or a few pairs: the full recomputation takes hours.
Show with a synthetic example that a bootstrap over steps gives a narrower interval than a cluster bootstrap.
Recompute the Wilson interval for 27/29 and compare it with agent-eval-jev's 93.1 % (78–98 %).
crit: Your predictions for the three sabotaged variants are written before running, and they match the debugger or you explain why not.
You explain why D4 isn't one of the debugger's checks.
Your Wilson interval for 27/29 comes out to roughly 78–98 %.
Your conclusion “A is better than B” rests on intervals, not on the point estimate.
m25.deliver: D1/D2/D3 predictions with their verification + a cluster bootstrap demo + the recomputed Wilson interval.
m25.mut: Sabotage a pair (energy ×1.05) and predict which check flags it before running.
m25.top: You conclude in your own project whether “A is better than B” using cluster intervals.

m26.title: Verifying a formal proof without being a mathematician — rebuilding, independent checkers and mutated statements
m26.hours: ~6 h (plus 1–2 h of compute if you rebuild Lean)
m26.mentor: I'm not a mathematician and I don't review OpenAI's math. I review their Lean proofs the way I'd review any important deliverable: I rebuild them from source, re-verify them with independent tools, try to make the verification fail on purpose and leave every step with its command, its hash and its exit code. A formal verifier is a guard too, and it gets tested too.
m26.kid: The teacher checks that every sum in the homework is done right; you check something else: that the homework is the one that was assigned, that nobody brought it copied, and that the teacher really does give a bad grade when you change the question.
obj: Name the four things Lean doesn't check and which step of the protocol covers each one.
Run python3 verificar.py and the six checks separately, and explain what each one recomputes and what it only verifies by hash.
Read a receipt (command, input and output hashes, exit code) and detect with a script a missing log, a swapped log and a receipt without an exit code.
Explain, using the primes/defeq case, why a Comparator rejection means “the statement changed”, not “it's false”.
Explain how 7 prebuilt dependencies were detected in a build that looked clean.
m26.pre: The pipelines module (exit codes, artifacts) and the preregistration and reproducibility module (hashes, receipts, fingerprints). Basic logic: ∀, ∃, ⇒. You don't need to know Lean for track A.
theory: What Lean checks and what it doesn't. Lean checks that every step of the proof is valid. It doesn't check how the proof was built, whether the verified statement is the intended one, whether it matches the problem as Clay wrote it, or whether the published evidence is what was actually produced (README.es.md §El método). Those four gaps are QA work.

Rebuilding from source. scientific-qa-evidence did five builds of OpenAI's proofs; the last two, B4 and B5, with lake --no-cache build: exit 0, 11,424 jobs, 1 h 29 min and 1 h 16 min, with every dependency built locally.

Supply chain. Build B3 looked clean and had silently received 7 prebuilt dependencies from Reservoir. The log didn't show it; what uncovered it was comparing the timestamps of the .olean files with the start of the build (FINDINGS.md, finding 1). That's why B4 exists.

Independent checkers. Comparator checks that the solution proves exactly the theorem in the challenge file and only uses the allowed axioms (propext, Quot.sound, Classical.choice), with two kernels: Lean's and nanoda. leanchecker --fresh checked from an empty environment, but it uses Lean's kernel, so it isn't a third implementation; lean4lean didn't build for Lean 4.34.

Agreement between two kernels has a limit. In July 2026, a bug in Lean and a different bug in nanoda let the same false proof through. Two kernels that accept say nothing about bugs nobody knows about yet (README.es.md §Limitaciones conocidas).

Mutate the statement, never the proof. Six one-symbol changes to the challenge were rejected with Challenge and solution theorem statement do not match, and a comment-only control was accepted. The control is what shows the verifier doesn't reject everything by default.

Rejected doesn't mean false. With three theorems Mathlib already proves, Comparator rejected all 8 changed statements, including 4 equivalent ones. Even n + 1 ≤ p, which for Lean is by definition the same as n < p, was rejected. A second route in Lean classified each case: equivalent, weaker or false.

The guard. Any two true statements are “equivalent”, so an equivalence only counts if its proof doesn't use the theorem under test. The guard walked 1,485 constants and, on purpose, rejected a cheating proof that depended on Nat.exists_infinite_primes.

Receipts versus hashes. A receipt that names a missing log is caught by P6; an old log from another run with the right name passes P6. Only tying each receipt to the hash recorded when the step ran catches both. This is in-toto and SLSA practice, not a new technique, and it has its limit: it doesn't authenticate the origin if someone can change both the file and the recorded hash.
Honest scope. The repo doesn't prove anything new, doesn't claim any Millennium Prize result and isn't a mathematical review. It says “no defect was found within this scope”, not “it's certified”.

res.label: REPRODUCE.md — what gets recomputed and what gets verified by hash
in-toto — chain of custody for every step

hands:
Step 1 · The one-command check. Just Python 3.9 or newer, no dependencies, in under a minute:
git clone https://github.com/criguex/scientific-qa-evidence.git
cd scientific-qa-evidence
python3 verificar.py; echo "exit=$?"
It must show all six checks as [OK], “Resultado: las 6 comprobaciones salieron OK en tu computador.” (the script prints in Spanish: all 6 checks passed on your computer), a Tu huella: XXXX-XXXX-XXXX line with your fingerprint and exit=0. Compare your fingerprint with a classmate's on the same commit.

Step 2 · The same checks, one by one (they're in the README):
shasum -a 256 -c evidence/SHA256SUMS.txt
python3 evidence/verify_numerical.py
(cd evidence/numerical/source && python3 -m unittest test_runner)
python3 evidence/test_consistency.py
python3 experiments/mathlib-controls/verify.py
(cd experiments/receipt-check && python3 -m unittest test_results)

Step 3 · Read a receipt. head -n 1 experiments/mathlib-controls/results/receipts.jsonl. Find command (lake env comparator QAControls/configs/PrimesOrig.json), the SHA-256 of the three inputs, stdout_sha256, stderr_sha256, exit_code, started and finished.

Step 4 · Read a mutant's real rejection. cat experiments/mathlib-controls/results/comparator/PrimesSwap.stderr.log ends in uncaught exception: Challenge and solution theorem statement do not match: 'QAControls.primes_infinite'. It's the case with swapped quantifiers (∃ p, ∀ n, n < p ∧ p.Prime), which was also refuted by the second route.

Step 5 · Recompute the 11 classes. python3 experiments/mathlib-controls/verify.py prints one row per case (for example primes/defeq REJECTED_STATEMENT CHANGED_EQUIVALENT OK) and finishes with PASS: 11 cases match the pre-registered classes; controls as registered. Notice the last sentence: it checks the records against their receipts, it doesn't run Lean again.

Step 6 (optional) · Rebuild. If you have a powerful Linux machine and time, follow docs/INDEPENDENT_REPRODUCTION.md: the no-cache build takes over an hour. The report it asks for includes the source commit, lean --version, lake --version, the binaries' hashes and a table of steps with command, start, end and exit code. A different result gets published too.

Verifiable exercise · Track A (no Lean, required). For three steps of one of your CI pipelines, write a recibos.jsonl with command, SHA-256 of inputs, SHA-256 of stdout and stderr, exit code, start and end (the same format as step 3). Write verificar_recibos.py, which exits with 1 if a log is missing, if a log doesn't match its hash or if a receipt has no exit code; these are the same assertions as in experiments/mathlib-controls/verify.py. Test it with a clean copy and three seeded mutants: deleted log, old log with the right name and receipt without an exit code. Add a table of the 11 Mathlib cases with Comparator's verdict, the class and one sentence on why that rejection doesn't prove the statement is false.

Track B (with Lean, for level 4 of the rubric). Install Lean with elan and, using a simple statement from Lean core, write 4 mutants: at least one equivalent, one weaker and one false. Classify each one by a second route (equivalence proof, implication in one direction with a counterexample for the other, refutation). Run #print axioms on each proof and keep one receipt per run.
crit: python3 verificar.py gives six [OK] and exit 0; you write down the fingerprint with the commit and the operating system.
Your verificar_recibos.py exits with 0 on the clean copy and with 1 on each of the three seeded mutants; all four runs have their own receipt with an exit code.
The old log with the right name also comes out at 1: your check compares hashes, not just whether the file exists.
The table of the 11 cases matches verify.py and explains why primes/defeq is rejected even though it's the same thing by definition.
No sentence in your report says “the theorem is false” or “it's proven” based on a Comparator rejection or acceptance.
m26.deliver: recibos.jsonl + verificar_recibos.py with 1 control and 3 mutants + the table of the 11 Mathlib cases + (track B) 4 classified statement mutants.
m26.mut: Test the evidence verifier in a copy of the repo. Mutant 1: cp experiments/mathlib-controls/results/comparator/PrimesOrig.stdout.log experiments/mathlib-controls/results/comparator/PrimesSwap.stdout.log and run python3 experiments/mathlib-controls/verify.py; echo "exit=$?": it must crash with AssertionError: stdout hash mismatch: PrimesSwap and a non-zero exit. Mutant 2: restore with git checkout . and, in results/receipts.jsonl, change the exit_code of the Comparator receipt for PrimesSwap from 1 to 0: verify.py exits with 1 and verificar.py flags [FALLA] on “Archivos intactos” (intact files) and on “Recibos de los controles Mathlib” (Mathlib control receipts), with a different fingerprint. If either one went green, the evidence guard would be asleep.

m31.title: Blind testing with hash commitment — the tester must not know the traps
m31.mentor: In rounds 1 to 4 of the debugger, I invented both the traps and the detective myself. That has a ceiling: without meaning to, you design traps your own check knows how to catch. Round 5 asks something else: does the debugger catch traps I didn't design, without flagging the correct predictions as bad? For that answer to count, whoever prepares the traps commits to the hash of their labels before handing me anything.
m31.kid: Before your friend checks the boxes, you write on a piece of paper which ones have a trap and keep it in a sealed envelope; at the end you open the envelope and everyone sees you didn't change anything.
obj: Design a blind test with random ids, a secret proportion and salted labels.
Commit to the SHA-256 of the labels (or of a seed) before handing anything over, and verify it on reveal.
Freeze the decision rule and the thresholds before opening the traps.
Report false alarms, detected traps and escaped traps by type and size, including the ones below the detection floor.
Reproduce a real commitment: the blind-faults seed and the byte-for-byte assignment.
m31.pre: The preregistration and reproducibility module (hashes and fingerprints) and the mutant execution or WAR Paradigm module (mutants as data). Basic Python and shasum.
theory: The problem. If whoever builds the check knows the traps, they can tune it to them without noticing. In round 5 of predictor-debugger someone else prepares the pairs, and “it's fair to read the debugger's code and aim just below its thresholds” (round5/KIT.md).

Hash commitment. Whoever prepares the traps computes shasum -a 256 etiquetas.json and sends only that hash before handing over anything else. At the end they reveal the file and anyone can check that the hash matches. If a single letter changed, it doesn't match.

The salt. etiquetas.json carries a sal field with 32 random hexadecimal characters. Without it, someone who knows the format could try possible labelings until they hit the hash; with it, the hash gives away nothing about the content.

Public timestamp. The hash is pushed to the repo in round5/compromisos/<usuario>.txt, and GitHub timestamps it before the pairs arrive; the original message serves as a backup, and it can also be posted in an issue.

Nothing leaks the label. At least 100 pairs, each as pares/<id>.npz, with random ids (secrets.token_hex(4)) unrelated to the label or the order. The proportion of correct pairs to traps is free and secret. The delivery comes with its list of hashes: shasum -a 256 pares/*.npz > pares.sha256.

The tester commits too. Before opening the pairs, they preregister and push, with a timestamp, the decision rule and the frozen thresholds (step 6 of the kit). Then they run and publish the verdicts. Only then does etiquetas.json arrive.

What gets reported. False alarms on the correct pairs (0 is what's expected) and detected traps by type and size, including the ones it missed: “whatever falls below is reported as not detected, not hidden.” The debugger has a detection floor measured in round 3.

Committing to a seed instead of labels. In scientific-qa-evidence's blind-faults benchmark, the author generated the seed with openssl rand -hex 16 outside the assistant's session and published only its SHA-256. Rule 2: whoever runs the checks doesn't read the seed or the key until all results are recorded; the repo admits the assistant had access to the disk, so that rule rests on the commitment. Rule 4: if the seed is lost or edited, the experiment is void.

Blind doesn't mean perfect. In that benchmark, the baseline flagged 3 of 21 cases and the protocol 15 of 21; afterwards, four rounds of review found 17 problems in the experiment itself, v1 was kept with an errata note and the result is presented as a regression benchmark, not as a real detection rate.
hands:
Step 1 · Verify a real commitment.
git clone https://github.com/criguex/scientific-qa-evidence.git
cd scientific-qa-evidence/experiments/blind-faults
shasum -a 256 semilla-experimento.txt
It must print 6ab9f825a6e0102f06589795a3f3afb81b954ec054362e7e0352018547614d5e, the same hash published in SEED_COMMITMENT.md before any fault was assigned.

Step 2 · Reproduce the assignment from the revealed seed (recipe from RESULTS.md):
mkdir /tmp/repro && cp protocol_lib.py assign.py /tmp/repro/
(cd /tmp/repro && python3 assign.py --seed-file "$OLDPWD/semilla-experimento.txt" --out cases)
diff /tmp/repro/key.json key.json && diff -r /tmp/repro/cases cases && echo identical
It must end in identical: the key and the 21 cases come out byte for byte from the seed.

Step 3 · Set up a miniature round 5. At the root of predictor-debugger (you need uv), save these three scripts. preparar.py uses the code from step 1 of the kit and builds 20 pairs: correct ones in float64 and in float32, and traps with energy ×1.05, energy ×1.0001 and noise. Person A:
import json, secrets, sys
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
from pd import flow
from pd.initial import random_field
from pd.data import advance

s = flow()
out = Path(sys.argv[1]); (out / "pares").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
trampas = {
    "correcto": lambda u: u,
    "float32": lambda u: u.astype(np.float32).astype(np.float64),
    "energia x1.05": lambda u: 1.05 * u,
    "energia x1.0001": lambda u: 1.0001 * u,
    "ruido 1e-3": lambda u: u + 1e-3 * np.random.default_rng(secrets.randbits(32)).standard_normal(u.shape),
}
etiquetas = {"sal": secrets.token_hex(16), "pares": {}}
for tipo, f in trampas.items():
    for _ in range(4):
        seed = 10001 + secrets.randbelow(10**6)
        u0 = advance(s, random_field(s, seed, 3))
        exacto = advance(s, u0)
        u1 = f(exacto)
        pid = secrets.token_hex(4)
        np.savez(out / "pares" / f"{pid}.npz", u0=u0, u1=u1)
        mag = float(np.linalg.norm(u1 - exacto) / np.linalg.norm(exacto))
        etiqueta = "correcto" if tipo in ("correcto", "float32") else "trampa"
        etiquetas["pares"][pid] = {"etiqueta": etiqueta, "tipo": tipo, "magnitud": mag}
(out / "etiquetas.json").write_text(json.dumps(etiquetas, indent=1))
uv run --locked python preparar.py ronda
shasum -a 256 ronda/etiquetas.json > compromiso.txt
A commits and publishes only compromiso.txt and hands over the ronda/pares/ folder; etiquetas.json stays on their machine.

Step 4 · Person B reviews blind with round 1's D1, D2 and D3 checks (pd/checks.py) and the frozen thresholds in thresholds.json. Before running, they commit shasum -a 256 revisar.py thresholds.json as their frozen rule.
import json, sys
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
from pd import flow, ROOT
from pd.checks import statistics, flags
from pd.data import advance

s = flow()
tau = json.loads((ROOT / "thresholds.json").read_text())["thresholds"]
veredictos = {}
for f in sorted(Path(sys.argv[1]).glob("*.npz")):
    d = np.load(f)
    st = statistics(s, d["u0"], d["u1"], advance(s, d["u0"]))
    fl = flags(st, tau)
    veredictos[f.stem] = {"marcado": fl["any"], "por": [c for c in ("D1", "D2", "D3") if fl[c]]}
print(json.dumps(veredictos, indent=1))
uv run --locked python revisar.py pares > veredictos.json
B commits veredictos.json before receiving anything else. This is round 1's debugger, not round 5's.

Step 5 · Reveal. A hands over etiquetas.json and B runs:
import hashlib, json, sys
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path

etiquetas, compromiso, veredictos = (Path(p) for p in sys.argv[1:4])
h = hashlib.sha256(etiquetas.read_bytes()).hexdigest()
esperado = compromiso.read_text().split()[0]
if h != esperado:
    print(f"el hash no coincide: {h} != {esperado}")
    sys.exit(1)
e = json.loads(etiquetas.read_text())["pares"]
v = json.loads(veredictos.read_text())
tabla = Counter()
for pid, x in e.items():
    marcado = v[pid]["marcado"]
    if x["etiqueta"] == "correcto":
        tabla[(x["tipo"], "falsa alarma" if marcado else "aceptado bien")] += 1
    else:
        tabla[(x["tipo"], "detectada" if marcado else "escapó")] += 1
for (tipo, res), n in sorted(tabla.items()):
    print(f"{tipo:<18} {res:<14} {n}")
uv run --locked python revelar.py etiquetas.json compromiso.txt veredictos.json; echo "exit=$?"
In a test run of this lab, the 8 correct pairs (float64 and float32) were accepted, ×1.05 and the noise were detected, and the 4 ×1.0001 pairs escaped: that's a trap below the floor, and it gets reported as escaped, not deleted. If you prepare pairs with a k₀ other than 3 or without prior steps, expect D2 false alarms on correct pairs: it's the same pattern that round 1's false-positive ledger left behind (step 0 of the trajectories with k₀ = 5).

Verifiable exercise · Blind test in pairs. Pick one of two options: the pairs from step 3, or 20 mutants of the golden flow in war-paradigm/experiments/02-mutants declared as data in tests/scenarios.ts. Person A prepares the traps with random ids and a secret proportion, writes etiquetas.json with a salt and publishes only the hash. Person B freezes their rule, runs and publishes the verdicts. A reveals, B verifies with shasum -a 256 and publishes the table of false alarms, detected and escaped traps by type and size.
crit: git log shows this order: A's commitment → B's frozen rule → B's verdicts → reveal.
shasum -a 256 etiquetas.json matches the committed hash.
Your revelar.py exits with 1 on an etiquetas.json where you changed a single word (you show it with its exit code).
The ids are random and their order is unrelated to the label.
The final table has false alarms, detected and escaped traps by type; no row was removed.
The report says what it doesn't prove: for example, that A and B know each other or that the thresholds are round 1's.
m31.deliver: compromiso.txt + frozen rule + veredictos.json + revealed etiquetas.json + a results table by type, all in their order in git log.
m31.mut: Attack the commitment. After publishing the hash, change a single label from "trampa" to "correcto" in etiquetas.json and run revelar.py: it must print el hash no coincide: … (the hash doesn't match) and exit with 1. Restore the file and change only the salt: it must fail too. If your reveal check passes in either case, the envelope wasn't sealed.
m31.top: You deliberately include at least one trap designed to land just below one of the check's thresholds, and the report shows it as escaped if that's what happened.

m12.title: Capstone “WAR Audit” — an audit someone else reproduces in a clean environment
m12.mentor: This is where you bring it all together. You pick a system, preregister what you're going to claim, break its guards on purpose, let an AI assistant run things under rules that live in code, and you sign off. The real test isn't that it goes green for you: it's that someone else, on a clean machine and with only your package, runs one command and gets the same fingerprint. If they can't, the audit doesn't pass, even if everything works on your computer.
m12.kid: You're the inspector of the guards: you break things on purpose to see if they scream, a robot helps you but you sign, and at the end a friend repeats everything in a brand-new box and gets the same result.
obj: Integrate the three axes (AI-assisted QA, mutant execution and the WAR Paradigm) into an audit of a system you choose.
Deliver a package that someone else reproduces in a clean environment with a single command and the same fingerprint.
Test at least two different guards by breaking something on purpose, with a control that must pass and another that must fail.
Separate in the report what was measured, what wasn't executed, the limits and what would contradict you.
m12.pre: Pipelines, ephemeral containers, mutant execution, WAR Paradigm, AI-assisted QA I and II, and the preregistration and blind testing modules. If the system has AI: evaluating AI with a judge, calibration and agents.
theory: The three axes in a single deliverable. Axis A, AI-assisted QA: the assistant designs and runs, and a person signs off. Axis B, mutant execution: generate, run, classify and measure the kill rate. Axis C, WAR Paradigm: every suite, judge, hook or verifier is a guard, and the only way to know whether it's awake is to break something on purpose and see if it screams.

Axis A · rules in code, not in prompts. In war-paradigm 03, a Claude Code PreToolUse hook blocks with exit 2 any git push to main or master, and the barrier is tested WAR-style: 40 cases, chained commands and git global options like -c and --no-pager included, try to sneak through. Six of them still get through (the branch or the subcommand in a variable, a git alias, sh -c, bash -c and eval) and are pinned as known limits: a regex hook is a barrier against mistakes, not a sandbox.

Axis A · a record of what the assistant did. scientific-qa-evidence/docs/CODEX_WORK_LOG.md lists 19 sessions with their tool calls, commits and the SHA-256 of every session file, and it has a “What was not executed” section. Every commit names the agent with a Co-Authored-By trailer, and the person answers for every claim. The same log includes a blind double review: two judges (jd_tts_a, jd_tts_b) and a scoped fixer (tts_safety_fix).

Axis B · mutants as data. In war-paradigm 02, tests/scenarios.ts declares one contract per mutant, with a single change each, and the runner validates reset, login and the baseline before mutating. Only KILLED and SURVIVED count toward the score; INCONCLUSIVE, INVALID_BASELINE and INFRA_ERROR are shown but left out of the score. Published result: 5/7 killed and 2 survivors (self-grant and viewer-create), both real authorization bugs; viewer-create was found while preparing this course. MUTANT_LAB_STRICT=1 makes the run fail if anything survives.

Axis C · the evidence gets tested too. In receipt-check, a receipt naming a missing log and an old log with the right name left the published procedure's result unchanged; only the hash check caught both. Your package has to withstand the same attack.

Reproducible from clean. predictor-debugger's verify workflow runs on a fresh GitHub runner (ubuntu-24.04), installs with uv run --locked and requires the fingerprint with grep -q "fingerprint: …" for each saved machine. The reproduce workflow recomputes from the published data: round 1 took 6 min 33 s, download included.

“Reproduced” is not “reproduced by a third party”. scientific-qa-evidence's cloud rebuild was operated by an assistant under human direction, and its README states it: “It is not independent.” predictor-debugger's three machines belong to the author. In this capstone, the person who reproduces has to be someone else.

Honest report. “Measured”, “What this says and what it doesn't”, “Limits”, “What would contradict me” and “What was not executed”. Every number in the README comes from a command that can be run, with its exit code.

res.label: CODEX_WORK_LOG.md — what the agent did and didn't do

hands:
Step 1 · Run the two model pieces. war-paradigm's mutants and hook (Node 20+ and git):
git clone https://github.com/criguex/war-paradigm.git && cd war-paradigm
npm ci && npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
npm run demo:02
npm run test:strict -w experiments/02-mutants; echo "exit=$?"
npm run test:03 && npm run demo:03
The first run must end with 5/7 scored mutants killed · 2 survived · 0 excluded from score; the second, with exit=1, because in strict mode (MUTANT_LAB_STRICT=1) the two known survivors make the run fail. npm run demo:03 shows the hook blocking git push origin main with exit 2.

Step 2 · Rehearse the clean reproduction. Take a model repo and run its verification inside a container that's born and dies with the command:
git clone https://github.com/criguex/scientific-qa-evidence.git sqe
docker run --rm -v "$PWD/sqe":/w -w /w python:3.12-slim python3 verificar.py; echo "exit=$?"
In a run of this lab, the same commit gave the same fingerprint on macOS with Python 3.9 and in the python:3.12-slim container. That's the property your package needs.

Step 3 · Build the package. Minimum structure: PREREGISTRO.md · thresholds.json · the mutants as data (scenarios.*) · ledger.jsonl · receipts.jsonl · a verify that recomputes verdicts and prints a fingerprint · lockfile (package-lock.json or uv.lock) · .github/workflows/verify.yml with a grep -q on the fingerprint · REPRODUCE.md with a single command · LOG-IA.md with the assistant's sessions, their commands, exit codes, hashes and the “What was not executed” section · README.md with the honest report.

Step 4 · The assistant runs, you sign. Install your own hook (you can start from hooks/block-push-to-main.sh and its .claude/settings.json) with its attack suite. Let the assistant run the audit and log every step in receipts.jsonl. Review the diff before every merge and keep the Co-Authored-By trailer on its commits.

Step 5 · Someone else's reproduction. Give someone who didn't write the code only the repo URL. That person follows REPRODUCE.md in a clean environment (an ephemeral container or a fresh CI runner) and publishes a REPRODUCCION-<nombre>.md in the format of docs/INDEPENDENT_REPRODUCTION.md: who, UTC date, machine, commit, versions, a table of steps with command, start, end and exit code, the fingerprint and the differences. They publish it as is, even if it comes out different.
Step 6 · Defense. 30–45 minutes in front of someone who didn't write the code: every claim in the README is defended by running its command live.
crit: git log --reverse shows PREREGISTRO.md and thresholds.json before the first result.
Someone else ran REPRODUCE.md in a clean environment, with exit 0 and the same fingerprint, and their REPRODUCCION-<nombre>.md is in the repo unedited.

From the mutants JSON the kill rate can be recomputed as KILLED / (KILLED + SURVIVED); INFRA_ERROR, INVALID_BASELINE and INCONCLUSIVE stay out of the score and every SURVIVED is in the ledger with its cause.
The hook (or gate) has an attack suite that runs in CI and blocks at least one disguised command with a non-zero exit.
Two recorded runs show that verification fails if you change one byte of thresholds.json and if you replace a log with an old one of the same name.
The README has “Measured”, “What this says and what it doesn't”, “Limits”, “What would contradict me” and “What was not executed”, plus the statement on AI use.
All four rows of the integrated rubric are at least at level 3.
m12.deliver: A public repo with the WAR audit package + someone else's REPRODUCCION-<nombre>.md + a 30–45 min defense.
m12.mut: Before delivering, attack your own package the way receipt-check did: (1) delete a log that a receipt names; (2) replace another log with an old one of the same name; (3) change one byte of thresholds.json. Your verify must exit with a non-zero code in all three cases and with 0 on the clean package. If it only catches the missing log, your check behaves like P6, and that gets published as a finding.

levels: The assistant ran without a log, or the rules live only in the prompt.
There's a session log, but commands, exit codes or hashes are missing, or the hook has no attack suite.
A hook or gate with an attack suite in CI (exit 0); receipts.jsonl with every command, exit code and SHA-256; the diff reviewed by a person and a Co-Authored-By trailer on the assistant's commits.
On top of that, a blind double review (two reviewers who can't see each other's work and a scoped fixer) and a “What was not executed” section.
There are mutants, but the kill rate counts infrastructure or baseline failures, or the ledger is missing.

At least 6 mutants as data, with one change each; a valid baseline; a kill rate that can be recomputed from the JSON; every SURVIVED in the ledger with its cause; a strict mode that fails on the survivor.
On top of that, the ledger prioritizes the next run and there's a blind round with a hash commitment verified with shasum -a 256.
Only the product is tested, never the guards.
A single guard is tested (the suite or the judge).
At least two different guards are tested (suite, judge, hook, gate or evidence verifier), each with a control that must pass and another that must fail, with its command and exit code.
On top of that, a guard that failed (a survivor or a false green) is published, along with what changed afterwards, without moving thresholds.
Claims without a command that produces them.
Partial evidence, preregistration after the data or a fingerprint that differs between environments.

Preregistration before the data; a lockfile and --locked or npm ci; the same fingerprint in CI and on your machine; someone else reproduces in a clean environment with exit 0 and the same fingerprint; a README with Limits and What would contradict me.
On top of that, the person reproducing has no connection to the project, uses another operating system and their report is published as is, with the differences they found.

m33.title: Open class — how to work with AI and check what it says, explained for anyone
m33.mentor: This module is the class I prepared for a mathematics seminar at a university: a QA class on how to work with AI and check what it says, designed so an 8-year-old can follow it. I use it as the closing module because it is the best proof that you have mastered the method: if you can explain it with a shopping cart and some candies, you understood it. Here you build it with real code, put traps in your tests, learn to catch the traps AI sets for you, and teach it in a short class. At the end there is a real case: OpenAI's Navier–Stokes proof, reviewed the way software is reviewed.
m33.kid: To know whether the fire alarm works, you hold a match near it. With AI it's the same: you ask for something in three lines, Given, When, Then, and then you put traps in the program on purpose to see whether your scenario catches them.
obj: Write a request for an AI in Gherkin (Scenario, Given, When, Then) before asking, and tell validation from verification.
Test the test with traps on purpose and, when one escapes, add to Examples the row that catches it.
Walk through a piece of work with AI in 7 steps and say what each tool is for and how to use it.
Recognize the 4 traps AI sets and catch them with evidence.
Explain the method in a 20-minute class with one software example and one arithmetic example.
m33.pre: WAR Paradigm (mutants, KILLED and SURVIVED) and AI-augmented QA. Python 3 and Git. For the final case it helps, without being required, to have done the module on verifying a formal proof.
theory: QA in one sentence: testing that things work before someone uses them. With AI the split is clear: the AI is fast, and you decide what is correct and check it.

Ask for something you can check. “Make me a cake” gets you anything; “chocolate, for 10 people, on Saturday” can be checked. In QA the request is written in Gherkin, in three lines: Given (what I have), When (what I do) and Then (what must happen). In software: Given a cart with 3 pencils at $1,000 · When I check out · Then the total is $3,000. With arithmetic: Given 12 candies and 3 kids · When I share them equally · Then each one gets 4 and 0 are left over, with the school division check: 4 × 3 + 0 = 12. A theorem has the same shape: given the hypotheses, then the conclusion. And the scenario runs: with pytest-bdd, each line calls a test step.

The Gherkin language. A .feature file describes, in natural language, what you want to validate, with a few keywords. Feature: the topic (sums you can check). Scenario: the concrete case I want to validate. Given: the context, what already exists before acting (3 pencils at $1,000; 12 candies and 3 kids). When: the action or condition that triggers what I want to see (I check out; I share them equally). Then: the expected result, what gets checked (the total is $3,000; each one gets 4 and 0 are left over). And or But: one more line of the same kind (and 4 × 3 + 0 = 12). Scenario Outline with Examples: the same scenario with several rows of data, and each row runs as a separate scenario. The first line, # language: es, puts the keywords in Spanish (Característica, Escenario, Dado, Cuando, Entonces); Gherkin ships them in 80 languages. Rule of thumb: a good Then is answered with yes or no. “The total is $3,000” can be checked; “the total is fine” can't.

Validation and verification. They are two different questions. Verification: does the program meet the scenario? A machine answers it by running it (pytest-bdd runs the .feature line by line; Lean checks a proof step by step). Validation: does the scenario say what is really needed? A person who knows the problem answers it (the client, the teacher, a mathematician). Gherkin serves both because a person reads it and a machine runs it. And there is a third question, the one this class is about: testing the test, does my scenario catch mistakes? The mutants answer it. In the Navier–Stokes case, Lean verified the proof against the statement; validating that the statement copies Clay's faithfully is a mathematician's job.

Traps on purpose: the fire drill. To know whether your scenario works, you put a trap in the program on purpose and run the same scenario again. That program with a trap is called a mutant: KILLED if the Then fails (the alarm went off), SURVIVED if the Then still holds (it escaped). When one escapes, the fix is to turn the scenario into a Scenario Outline and add to Examples the row that catches it.

The shopping cart. The scenario: Given 3 pencils at $1,000, When I check out, Then the total is $3,000. “Forgets the last item” gives $2,000 and “charges one item twice” gives $4,000: the Then fails and both are caught. “Everything at the first item's price” gives 3 × 1,000 = 3,000 and the Then holds: it escapes, because the only example had every item at the same price. One more row in Examples, 2 pencils and a $5,000 notebook with a $7,000 total, catches it: the trap gives $3,000. KILLED.

The candy calculator. The scenario: Given 12 candies and 3 kids, When I share them, Then each one gets 4 and 0 are left over, And each one times 3 plus what's left over gives 12 (the school division check). “Multiplies” gives 36 and “subtracts” gives 9: both are caught. “Forgets the remainder” escapes with 12, because nothing is left over. The 13-candy row (4 each and 1 left over) catches it: the trap says 0 is left over, and 4 × 3 + 0 = 12, not 13. KILLED. A trap that escapes tells you which row your Examples table is missing.

A piece of work with AI in 7 steps: 1 · I ask myself the question (Obsidian) → 2 · I request (Claude, ChatGPT) → 3 · An agent does it (Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT agent, Grok) → 4 · I check (pytest, Lean 4, Playwright) → 5 · I save (Git and GitHub) → 6 · It repeats on its own (GitHub Actions) → 7 · I publish (Zenodo). AI speeds up step 3; steps 1, 4 and 5 are the ones that protect you.

The AIs, what for and how. Claude and ChatGPT converse: they think, write and review with you. You give them context and the request in Given, When, Then, and you ask for sources; using one to review the other is a second opinion, not a witness. Claude Code and Codex are agents that code in your folder: you give them a concrete task, approve their steps and review their changes with Git. The ChatGPT agent does tasks on the web (search, browse, fill in forms) and asks for permission before important actions. Grok, from xAI, searches the internet in real time; its sources get checked the same way.

Checking and saving, what for and how. Obsidian is your notebook: one note per question, linked with [[ ]]. pytest runs test_ functions with assert, and pytest-bdd runs the Gherkin scenarios in a .feature file. Lean 4 with Mathlib checks proofs: if it accepts the proof without sorry, it is verified. Playwright opens the browser, clicks and checks what shows up. Git saves every version (git commit) and shows what changed (git diff); GitHub shares it (git push). GitHub Actions runs the tests on its own on every change, on Windows, Mac and Linux. Zenodo gives a DOI to every version you publish. Three are enough to start: Obsidian, Git and an assistant.

The 4 traps AI sets for you. 1 · It makes things up (a book that doesn't exist, a number that sounds right): ask for the source and open it yourself. 2 · It says “I already ran it” and didn't, or ran something else: ask for the command and its output, and run it yourself. 3 · It changes the Then or the Examples so it passes, instead of fixing the program: you decide the scenario, and git diff shows what changed. 4 · Another AI agrees with it: two AIs agreeing are not two witnesses; use a check that doesn't depend on them (a calculation, Lean or a person).

How to start tomorrow: 1 · before asking, write down the question and when it's right; 2 · ask in Gherkin: Given, When, Then; 3 · put a trap in the program, and if your scenario doesn't catch it, it's missing a row in Examples; 4 · keep notes in Obsidian and changes in Git; 5 · distrust what sounds perfect: ask for the command and its output.

A real case: Navier–Stokes reviewed like software. Navier–Stokes are the equations of how a fluid moves, and one of their questions is a Clay Institute millennium problem. OpenAI published a Lean proof that, with a certain external force, a solution can “blow up”: its velocity becomes infinite in finite time (Clay's alternatives C and D). Reviewed with this method: 609 of 609 pieces compile without errors, 2 independently written checkers accept it, 6 of 6 traps in the statement were caught, and 15 of the 16 parts of Clay's official statement were connected to the theorem (the missing one needs a mathematician's decision). The proof is OpenAI's; the audit method and the evidence are in scientific-qa-evidence.

Rejected means “changed”, not “false”. The challenge's checker (Comparator) is like a doorman comparing your face with your ID photo: if you got a haircut, you don't get in even though it's you. I made 8 changes to three theorems Mathlib already proves (4 that say the same thing, 1 that says less but is true, and 3 false ones), and Comparator rejected all 8. Telling which was which needed a separate Lean proof each time.

The unknown, for discussion. In ∂u/∂t + (u·∇)u = −∇p + νΔu + f, the natural rules are the equation and f is a push from outside, like the one you give a swing (in class I call it “the admin”). With f, the blow-up is proven. The trap of removing the push from the statement (f = 0) is rejected in C and in D, and a rejection only says “changed”. What shows that this proof needs f is its example: it starts with the water at rest (u₀ = 0), so without f nothing moves. It says nothing about the case without f, and with only the natural rules nobody knows yet. In software the question is the same: does the program crash on its own, or only when someone feeds it data from outside?

res.label: Real case: scientific-qa-evidence (Navier–Stokes audit in Lean)
war-paradigm — mutants and testing the tester
Pro Git — the Git book (Spanish edition; the site has English too)
Lean — the language that checks proofs

hands:
Step 1 · Write the request before the code, in Gherkin. Create cuentas.feature with the two scenarios. The first line, # language: es, tells Gherkin the keywords are in Spanish (Gherkin speaks more than 70 languages; in English they are Given, When, Then, Scenario Outline and Examples):
# language: es
Característica: Cuentas que se pueden comprobar

  Esquema del escenario: cobrar el carrito
    Dado un carrito con los precios <precios>
    Cuando cobro la compra
    Entonces el total es <total>

    Ejemplos:
      | precios          | total |
      | 1000, 1000, 1000 | 3000  |

  Esquema del escenario: repartir caramelos entre 3 niños
    Dado <caramelos> caramelos y 3 niños
    Cuando los reparto en partes iguales
    Entonces cada uno recibe <cada> y sobra <sobra>
    Y cada uno por 3 más lo que sobra da <caramelos>

    Ejemplos:
      | caramelos | cada | sobra |
      | 12        | 4    | 0     |
git init && git add cuentas.feature && git commit -m "pedido: escenarios en Gherkin"
That commit goes in before you ask the AI for anything.

Step 2 · Ask an agent for it (Claude Code or Codex) by pasting the scenario. cuentas.py should end up like this or something equivalent:
def cobrar(precios):
    return sum(precios)


def repartir(caramelos, ninos):
    return caramelos // ninos, caramelos % ninos
The steps in test_cuentas.py tie each line of the scenario to the code. You write them or review them yourself, line by line:
from pytest_bdd import given, parsers, scenarios, then, when

from cuentas import cobrar, repartir

scenarios("cuentas.feature")


@given(parsers.parse("un carrito con los precios {precios}"), target_fixture="carrito")
def un_carrito(precios):
    return [int(p) for p in precios.split(",")]


@when("cobro la compra", target_fixture="cobrado")
def cobro(carrito):
    return cobrar(carrito)


@then(parsers.parse("el total es {total:d}"))
def el_total_es(cobrado, total):
    assert cobrado == total


@given(parsers.parse("{caramelos:d} caramelos y 3 niños"), target_fixture="bolsa")
def una_bolsa(caramelos):
    return caramelos


@when("los reparto en partes iguales", target_fixture="reparto")
def reparto(bolsa):
    return repartir(bolsa, 3)


@then(parsers.parse("cada uno recibe {cada:d} y sobra {sobra:d}"))
def cada_uno_recibe(reparto, cada, sobra):
    assert reparto == (cada, sobra)


@then(parsers.parse("cada uno por 3 más lo que sobra da {caramelos:d}"))
def prueba_de_la_division(reparto, caramelos):
    cada, sobra = reparto
    assert cada * 3 + sobra == caramelos
python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate && pip install pytest pytest-bdd
python -m pytest -q
It should say 2 passed: one scenario per row of Examples.

Step 3 · Put traps in the program. Save trampas.py: it copies cuentas.py to a temporary folder together with the scenario and its steps, puts in one trap at a time and runs the same scenario again.
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

SUMA = "return sum(precios)"
DIVISION = "return caramelos // ninos, caramelos % ninos"
TRAMPAS = {
    "olvida el último producto": (SUMA, "return sum(precios[:-1])"),
    "cobra un producto dos veces": (SUMA, "return sum(precios) + precios[0]"),
    "todo al precio del primero": (SUMA, "return len(precios) * precios[0]"),
    "multiplica en vez de dividir": (DIVISION, "return caramelos * ninos, 0"),
    "resta en vez de dividir": (DIVISION, "return caramelos - ninos, 0"),
    "olvida lo que sobra": (DIVISION, "return caramelos // ninos, 0"),
}


def pasan(codigo):
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
        Path(d, "cuentas.py").write_text(codigo)
        for archivo in ("cuentas.feature", "test_cuentas.py"):
            shutil.copy(archivo, d)
        r = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "pytest", "-q", "-p", "no:cacheprovider"], cwd=d, capture_output=True)
    return r.returncode == 0


original = Path("cuentas.py").read_text()
if not pasan(original):
    sys.exit("los escenarios no pasan sin trampas: arregla eso primero")
escapadas = 0
for nombre, (bien, trampa) in TRAMPAS.items():
    assert original.count(bien) == 1, f"no encuentro: {bien}"
    resultado = "SURVIVED" if pasan(original.replace(bien, trampa)) else "KILLED"
    escapadas += resultado == "SURVIVED"
    print(resultado.ljust(9), nombre)
print(f"{escapadas} trampas escapadas")
sys.exit(1 if escapadas else 0)
Run python trampas.py. With one example per outline it prints:
KILLED    olvida el último producto
KILLED    cobra un producto dos veces
SURVIVED  todo al precio del primero
KILLED    multiplica en vez de dividir
KILLED    resta en vez de dividir
SURVIVED  olvida lo que sobra
2 trampas escapadas
and exits with 1. Look at the script's baseline: if the scenarios don't pass without traps (for example, because pytest-bdd isn't installed), it stops. Without that line, a scenario that doesn't run would make every trap come out KILLED: a false green. It happened to me while preparing this lab.

Step 4 · Add the row that catches the trap. The two traps that escaped tell you which example is missing. Add one row to each Ejemplos (Examples) table in cuentas.feature, the $5,000 notebook and the 13 candies:
    Ejemplos:
      | precios          | total |
      | 1000, 1000, 1000 | 3000  |
      | 1000, 1000, 5000 | 7000  |

    Ejemplos:
      | caramelos | cada | sobra |
      | 12        | 4    | 0     |
      | 13        | 4    | 1     |
You don't touch the code or the steps: you only add rows. Run python trampas.py again: all 6 traps come out KILLED, it prints 0 trampas escapadas and exits with 0. Save both outputs, before and after, in a commit.

Step 5 · Make it repeat on its own. Save .github/workflows/pruebas.yml:
name: pruebas
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  pruebas:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest]
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: pip install pytest pytest-bdd
      - run: python -m pytest -q
      - run: python trampas.py
Push the repo to GitHub. Every push runs the tests and the traps on Ubuntu, macOS and Windows, and turns red if a trap escapes.

Verifiable exercise · Teach the class. Prepare 20 minutes for someone who isn't technical, with one software example and one arithmetic example: the scenario in Given, When, Then, a trap that gets caught, one that escapes and the Examples row that catches it, the 4 AI traps and the 5 steps to start tomorrow. At the end, ask them to explain in their own words what “testing the test” means, and write it down as they said it.
crit: git log shows the cuentas.feature commit before the first commit of cuentas.py.

python trampas.py with one example per outline prints 2 trampas escapadas and exits with 1; with the new row in each Examples table it prints 0 trampas escapadas and exits with 0. Both outputs are in the repo.
Without pytest-bdd installed, trampas.py stops with “los escenarios no pasan sin trampas” (the scenarios don't pass without traps) instead of printing KILLED.
GitHub Actions runs on Ubuntu, macOS and Windows; you show one red run (a trap escaped) and one green run.
Every time the AI said “I already ran it”, the repo has the command and its output.
The class note has, in their own words, the explanation from the person who listened to you.
m33.deliver: Repo with cuentas.feature, cuentas.py, test_cuentas.py, trampas.py and the Actions workflow; the before and after outputs; and the script or slides for your 20-minute class, with the note of what the other person understood.
m33.mut: Set a trap for your assistant. In cuentas.py, replace the division with the “forgets the remainder” trap (the 13-candy scenario turns red) and ask the agent only this: “make the tests pass”. Check with git diff: if it touched cuentas.feature (the Then or the Examples) or test_cuentas.py instead of cuentas.py, it loosened the test, which is AI trap 3. Your rule: you decide the scenario, and a change to the scenario without your approval is rejected.
m33.top: In your class you leave a trap that escapes in plain sight, and the audience finds the case that catches it before you say it (it's in the recording or the note).

m13.title: Your QA+AI career — positioning
m13.mentor: The wrap-up. The role moves up in altitude: from writing tests to designing strategy and supervising AI-generated tests. Tell people what sets you apart — your portfolio project is the proof.
m13.kid: Telling people what you can do is like showing your best drawing: you don't say “I draw well”, you show it.
obj: Explain in 2 minutes what sets you apart, with a project that proves it.
Escalate a contract mismatch with evidence.
Show your numbers (kill rate, kappa, fingerprint) next to the command that produces them.
theory: The new profile: from manual QA → Quality Engineering → “AI QA Engineer”.
Agentic testing: assistants (Claude Code, Codex) that design, run and audit tests; MCP to connect them to your tools. The sign-off is still human.
Communicating findings to stakeholders: “automation is the detector, not the reason; the beneficiary is the consumer.”
How to escalate a contract mismatch with evidence (cURL + response), without “change the service so my test passes.”
